Solutions 2 and 3 both include the subgroup of order $p-1$, but neither justifies it. Solution 1 rules that subgroup out with a concrete example: for $\mathbb{Z}_9$ with $H=\{\pm1\}$, the Terwilliger algebra is $M_5\oplus M_4$, which has a second non-commutative block and so is not almost commutative. I did not verify that decomposition independently, so my acceptance of Solution 1 rests on its analysis being consistent with the cases I could check.

Solution 1's three surviving subgroups are the trivial group (order 1), the Sylow $p$-subgroup (order $p^{n-1}$), and the full $\text{Aut}(G)$ (order $p^{n-1}(p-1)$). The trivial case gives $T=M_{p^n}$, which has a single, primary module, so it is consistent with almost commutativity. The sum $1+p^{n-1}+p^{n-1}(p-1)=p^n+1$ follows correctly from these orders.

The answer $p^n+1$ therefore appears correct. The main residual uncertainty is whether the trivial subgroup really belongs in the list, since that depends on the precise definition of "almost commutative" in the source.

VERDICT 1: ACCEPT
VERDICT 2: REJECT
VERDICT 3: REJECT
